pages.x: King John of England lost Normandy to the French king in 1204 and squeezed his barons for money to win it back. He quarrelled with the pope, who shut England's churches for six years. When his last war in France failed in 1214, the barons rebelled.

In May 1215 the rebels took London. John agreed to meet them on 15 June in a meadow by the Thames, at Runnymede, and set his seal on a long list of promises they had drawn up. It came to be called Magna Carta, the Great Charter.
One clause promised that no free man would be jailed or stripped of his rights except by the lawful judgement of his peers or by the law of the land.
pages.fx: Another said justice would not be sold, denied or delayed. Together they put in writing that the king himself was under the law.

pages.x: Neither side kept the deal. Within ten weeks the pope, at John's request, declared the charter void, and civil war broke out. John died in 1216 in the middle of it, after losing part of his baggage, perhaps with his jewels, in the tidal sands of the Wash.

To win back the barons, the men ruling for John's nine-year-old son, Henry III, issued the charter again in 1216, 1217 and 1225. Later kings confirmed it again and again, and it became part of English law.
Four copies of the 1215 charter survive, written in Latin on parchment: two in the British Library and one each in Lincoln and Salisbury cathedrals. No one signed it: King John sealed it.

Lawyers fighting the Stuart kings in the 1600s rediscovered Magna Carta, and settlers carried its ideas to America, where they echo in the Bill of Rights. In 1948 Eleanor Roosevelt hoped the new Universal Declaration of Human Rights would be a Magna Carta for all people everywhere.

Magna Carta failed as a peace treaty but lived on as an idea: that rulers are bound by the law and cannot jail people as they please. Only three of its clauses are still law in England, but it is honoured around the world as a foundation of freedom.
